pitfalls.readme_said: Build from source: git clone, cd caddy/cmd/caddy, go build (Go 1.26+)
pitfalls.actually_needed: I used the README's primary install instead: downloading the prebuilt binary from GitHub Releases. That avoids installing a Go toolchain.

pitfalls.readme_said: Caddy may bind to low ports; use sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service
pitfalls.actually_needed: Without root, set http_port 8080 and https_port 8443 in the global options and use skip_install_trust with tls internal. Then no setcap or sudo is needed.

pitfalls.readme_said: Dynamic configuration with the JSON API
pitfalls.actually_needed: POST /load replaces the whole running config, so sites from the Caddyfile stop serving until you reload the Caddyfile (command 11 failed with 'connection refused' after the load). This is how /load is meant to work.

judge.observed: Caddy served the Caddyfile response on port 8081, answered over HTTP/2 with TLS on 8443, and reported version v2.11.9.

features.feature: automatic HTTPS with ZeroSSL and Let's Encrypt
features.note: Getting ZeroSSL or Let's Encrypt certificates needs a public domain and the outside ACME servers. Only the local internal CA was exercised (command 7 log: 'certificate obtained successfully', issuer local).

what_it_does.quote: Fast and extensible multi-platform HTTP/1-2-3 web server with automatic HTTPS

who_it_is_for.quote: Caddy is most often used as an HTTPS server, but it is suitable for any long-running Go program.

prerequisites.quote: **Runs anywhere** with **no external dependencies** (not even libc)

install_per_os.quote:
$ git clone "https://github.com/caddyserver/caddy.git"
$ cd caddy/cmd/caddy/
$ go build

config_and_keys.quote: Nearly all of Caddy's configuration is contained in a single config document, rather than being scattered across CLI flags and env variables and a configuration file as with other web servers.

troubleshooting_uninstall.quote: On Linux, this can be done easily with: `sudo setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep ./caddy`
